summary: Reports on a meeting held at an IETF gathering in Houston in November 1993 about the future of white pages directory services for the Internet. It records the discussion and the approaches considered. It is a meeting report, not a protocol specification.

eli5.summary: Some grown-ups met to talk about how to build a big phone book for the Internet. This note writes down what they said.

subtitle: A meeting report on Internet directory services for finding people

tldr.problem: The Internet needed a standardized white pages directory to help people find contact information for other users, but deployment of X.500 directory services had been slow due to complexity, lack of infrastructure, and competing technologies.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC reports on a November 1993 IETF meeting that discussed four key questions: what functions white pages services should provide, what technologies could support them, what problems needed solving, and what deployment strategy would work.
tldr.outcome: The meeting recommended adopting a common-ground approach that supports multiple technologies and protocols, with X.500 as a core complemented by simpler services like Whois++ and index servers, along with central infrastructure management.

facts.label: Main use case
facts.value: Finding contact information and security certificates

facts.label: Protocols discussed
facts.value: X.500, LDAP, Whois++, Netfind, DNS, Gopher, WAIS

today: RFC 1588 is an Informational document and a historical snapshot of directory service thinking in 1993. The common-ground approach it recommended proved prescient: LDAP became the standard lightweight protocol for directory access, X.500 deployments remained limited but continued in specialized environments, and modern systems use DNS, LDAP, and web-based lookup for finding people and services. The security certificate storage recommendation was addressed by the growth of Public Key Infrastructures (PKIs) and certificate authorities.

sections.title: The Need for Internet Directories
sections.content: A white pages service is a directory that helps people find contact information for other individuals: email addresses, postal addresses, phone numbers, or even security certificates for encryption. As the Internet grew, finding someone became harder. This RFC reports on a November 1993 meeting organized by USC/ISI to discuss how to provide white pages services for the Internet. The meeting examined X.500, an international directory standard, as a potential solution and considered alternatives. An electronic mail discussion preceded the in-person meeting to gather views from the community.
sections.eli5: When you need to find someone's email address or phone number, you need a directory. The meeting was about how to build one that works for the whole Internet.

sections.title: Functions and Requirements
sections.content: A white pages directory must perform two core functions: searching and retrieval. Searching means finding people given partial or fuzzy information, such as "Find Postel in southern California." Retrieval means obtaining detailed information about a person once found, such as email address, phone, postal address, or security certificate. Certificates are particularly important for emerging secure applications like Privacy Enhanced Mail (PEM), which require directory support. The meeting also identified that users want fast searching across distributed databases, even on attributes different from the database's structure, which typically requires pre-computed indices. A white pages directory should be flexible, have low resource requirements, fit into existing systems, be low-cost, and provide reliable responses suitable for automated tools.
sections.eli5: A white pages needs to let you search for people in different ways (by name, location, organization) and show you their contact information. It also needs to store security certificates for encryption.

sections.title: Existing Technologies and Approaches
sections.content: Multiple technologies existed for directory services. X.500 is an international standard offering a distributed, flexible, hierarchical architecture with security and replication. It can serve both humans and applications. However, X.500 implementations were complex and difficult to install, particularly the quipu reference implementation. LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) provided a simpler client-side alternative. Other services like Whois++ offered a simpler but less comprehensive approach, Netfind used proactive data gathering, and Gopher and WAIS had been successfully deployed for other information services. The meeting recognized that no single solution would suffice; instead, bridging among different systems through gateways (Gopher to X.500, Whois++ to X.500, WWW to X.500) offered practical benefit. The challenge was that white pages services, unlike Gopher or WAIS, must provide correct answers a high percentage of the time to be considered successful by users.
sections.eli5: Different directory systems existed: X.500 was powerful but complicated, LDAP was simpler, and others like Whois++ were specialized. The answer was to let them work together through gateways.

sections.title: Technology Problems and Infrastructure Gaps
sections.content: The RFC identified two classes of problems. Technology issues included the difficulty of X.500 software: implementations were large and complex, had high resource requirements, and were hard to install. The public domain quipu implementation was not production-ready. Client-side work was also needed, including building directory access into applications like email and building effective search tools. The ISODE Consortium was developing improvements but these had not yet reached widespread deployment. Infrastructure problems were equally serious: X.500 lacked central management (the DNS has a clear root; X.500 did not), naming rules were not standardized, and sites needed assistance connecting to the system. The RFC noted that data population (finding, converting, and maintaining accurate information about people) was inherently difficult regardless of the protocol chosen. Deployment of X.500 in the United States had slowed after the end of the FOX project, which had provided infrastructure support.
sections.eli5: X.500 software was hard to set up and maintain. Nobody was clearly in charge of managing the whole system. Getting accurate information about people and keeping it updated was hard work.

sections.title: Deployment Strategy and Recommendations
sections.content: The report recommended a common-ground approach that encourages multiple client and server types with standardized interoperation protocols, supporting simple clients, front-ends like Gopher, and embedded access in applications. This allows users to choose their own level of complexity and entry cost. The meeting suggested developing index-servers with multiple search methods to address the yellow pages problem. X.500 should be retained as a core infrastructure with central management support—comparable to the effort for maintaining DNS roots—but complemented with simpler services. The report noted that Internet services that gained momentum, like WAIS and Gopher, followed a pattern: small groups built practical software, the community adopted it as a de facto standard, then formalized it. The RFC emphasized that technical specifications alone are insufficient; the solution must fit how the Internet community actually adopts technology. The greatest impact on X.500 adoption came from the Gopher gateway, showing that ease of access is crucial. The report urged continued investment in X.500 infrastructure, improved software, and better procedures for connecting sites.
sections.eli5: Let many different systems work together. Make it easy to get started. Keep the whole system managed like the DNS. Let services evolve naturally instead of forcing one solution.
